stem: In a well-governed CMDB, who is accountable for defining policy, standards, and the data model — the strategic ownership of CMDB data quality across the organization?

options.text: The CMDB Data Manager, who runs scheduled retirement and archival jobs
The CMDB / Configuration Management governance board
Discovery, which auto-populates CIs and therefore owns their accuracy
Individual assignment groups that happen to use the CIs day to day

rationale: Governance is a people-and-process responsibility before it is a tool. ServiceNow's CMDB governance model puts a governance board / CMDB owner at the top: they set policy, define standards, approve the data model, and hold accountability for data quality. Tools like Data Manager and Discovery execute against that policy — they don't define it.

distractor_notes.A: The Data Manager is an execution tool (and an operational role) for lifecycle actions; it carries out policy, it doesn't author it.
distractor_notes.C: Discovery is an ingestion source. Automating population doesn't make it the accountable owner of quality or standards.
distractor_notes.D: Consumers of CIs provide input and may attest to accuracy, but org-wide standards and policy sit with governance, not scattered groups.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: You need to automatically retire CIs that Discovery has not seen for 90 days, then delete them 30 days after that — applied consistently and at scale. Which tool is purpose-built for this?

options.text: CMDB Data Manager (lifecycle management policies)
A scheduled script that deletes rows from cmdb_ci directly
CMDB Health dashboard remediation
The Identification and Reconciliation Engine

rationale: CMDB Data Manager exists precisely to manage the CI lifecycle — defining policies and rules that move CIs through stages such as retire, then archive or destroy/delete, on conditions like 'last discovered' age. It applies actions consistently across large CI populations without ad-hoc scripting.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting rows directly skips relationship cleanup, audit, and the lifecycle states Data Manager manages — it's exactly the un-governed approach Data Manager replaces.
distractor_notes.C: Health remediation surfaces and fixes quality issues; it isn't the scheduled lifecycle (retire/archive/delete) engine.
distractor_notes.D: IRE identifies and reconciles incoming data into CIs; it doesn't run retirement/deletion lifecycle policies.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: In CMDB Data Manager, what is the difference between archiving a CI and destroying (deleting) it?

options.text: Archiving removes the CI immediately; destroying keeps a copy in an archive table
Archiving moves the CI out of active tables but retains a recoverable copy
They are identical — both just set the CI's install_status to Retired
Archiving applies only to relationships; destroying applies only to attributes

rationale: Lifecycle actions escalate in finality. Archive moves the CI off the active tables into archive storage so it's out of operational use but still recoverable for audit/compliance. Destroy/delete permanently removes the record. Retire is a softer state change that precedes both.

distractor_notes.A: Reversed. Archiving retains a recoverable copy; it does not remove immediately and irreversibly.
distractor_notes.C: Retiring is a state change; archive and destroy are distinct data actions, not synonyms for setting Retired.
distractor_notes.D: Both actions operate on the CI record as a whole, not selectively on relationships vs attributes.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Data Certification in the context of CMDB governance?

options.text: To discover new CIs on the network automatically
To schedule tasks asking responsible users to verify that specified CI data is accurate and up to date
To merge duplicate CIs detected by the identification engine
To calculate the CMDB Health completeness score

rationale: Data Certification is a governance control that periodically generates certification tasks (filters) and routes them to accountable users to confirm — or correct — that the data still reflects reality. It's how an organization keeps human-maintained data honest between automated scans.

distractor_notes.A: That's Discovery. Certification verifies existing data; it doesn't probe the network.
distractor_notes.C: Merging duplicates is de-duplication / IRE remediation, not certification.
distractor_notes.D: Completeness scoring is a CMDB Health (Insight) function; certification is a manual attestation process.

stem: Within the Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE), what is the role of an identification rule?

options.text: It decides which data source is authoritative for each attribute
It uses identifier entries
It defines how long a CI is retained before deletion
It controls which users can edit a CI class

rationale: Identification rules answer the question 'is this the same CI I already have?' Each rule contains one or more identifier entries whose criterion attributes (e.g., serial number, name) are matched against existing records to identify an exact match, create a new CI, or flag a duplicate.

distractor_notes.A: That's a reconciliation rule's job — deciding the authoritative source per attribute.
distractor_notes.C: Retention/deletion is Data Manager lifecycle, not identification.
distractor_notes.D: Edit access is controlled by roles/ACLs, not IRE identification rules.

stem: What does a reconciliation rule in IRE control?

options.text: Which discovery source (data source) is allowed to write a given attribute, so authoritative data isn't overwritten by a lesser source
Whether two CIs should be merged into one
The order in which CI classes appear in CI Class Manager
The frequency of CMDB Health scans

rationale: Reconciliation rules enforce data authority. When multiple sources write to the same CI, the reconciliation rule names which source 'owns' a particular attribute (or set of attributes), so a less authoritative integration can't clobber values maintained by the authoritative one.

distractor_notes.B: Matching/merging is identification, not reconciliation. Reconciliation arbitrates updates once a CI is identified.
distractor_notes.C: CI Class Manager display order has nothing to do with IRE reconciliation.
distractor_notes.D: Health scan scheduling is a separate dashboard configuration.

stem: Two integrations both insert a server CI, but because of slightly different names IRE creates two records for the same physical host. What governance artifact is generated so this can be remediated?

options.text: A CMDB Health completeness alert
A de-duplication task (duplicate CI remediation)
A data certification filter
A reconciliation rule exception

rationale: When IRE detects records that resolve to the same real-world item, it raises de-duplication tasks. These drive a remediation workflow where an administrator confirms the duplicate set and merges them, collapsing the records into a single CI and preserving relationships.

distractor_notes.A: Completeness measures missing attributes, not duplicate identity collisions.
distractor_notes.C: Certification asks humans to verify data; it isn't the duplicate-merge mechanism.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation governs attribute authority; it doesn't itself create a remediation task for duplicates.

stem: The Configuration Management / CMDB Workspace gives a CMDB manager a single place to do which of the following?

options.text: Only view raw cmdb_ci table rows
Monitor CMDB health, triage remediation, and manage CI data from a role-based workspace
Write Discovery patterns
Configure email notifications for incidents

rationale: The CMDB Workspace is the manager's cockpit: health KPIs, remediation queues, and data management surfaced together so a configuration manager can see quality problems and act on them without hopping across disparate modules.

distractor_notes.A: It's far more than a table view — it's an analytics-and-action workspace.
distractor_notes.C: Pattern authoring lives in Discovery / Pattern Designer, not the CMDB manager workspace.
distractor_notes.D: Incident notifications are an ITSM concern, unrelated to the CMDB workspace's purpose.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: A CMDB Data Manager policy is configured but you want to confirm what it will affect before it runs destructive actions. What is the recommended safe practice?

options.text: Run the policy in preview/dry-run to see the impacted CIs before committing
Delete a few CIs manually first to test
Disable IRE while the policy runs
Turn off CMDB Health scans during execution

rationale: Lifecycle actions can be destructive, so Data Manager lets you preview the population a policy targets before it executes. Reviewing the impacted set first is the governance-minded way to avoid retiring or destroying CIs you didn't intend to.

distractor_notes.B: Manual deletion bypasses the very lifecycle governance you're trying to validate and risks orphaned relationships.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling IRE doesn't validate the policy and would harm ongoing reconciliation.
distractor_notes.D: Health scans are unrelated to validating which CIs a lifecycle policy targets.

stem: Which statement best describes why CMDB governance is described as 'a program, not a project'?

options.text: Because the CMDB is configured once and never changes
Because data quality requires ongoing policy, ownership
Because only the project team is ever allowed to edit CIs
Because governance applies only during the initial Discovery rollout

rationale: A CMDB decays without continuous care — environments change, sources drift, duplicates creep in. Governance is therefore a standing program: defined owners, recurring certification, health monitoring, and lifecycle management that persist long after the implementation 'project' ends.

distractor_notes.A: The opposite is true — the environment changes constantly, which is exactly why governance must be ongoing.
distractor_notes.C: Governance defines who maintains data, but it isn't about freezing edit rights to a project team forever.
distractor_notes.D: Governance must outlive the rollout; limiting it to initial Discovery is how CMDBs rot.

stem: What is a CI Identifier (cmdb_identifier) in the IRE framework?

options.text: A unique sys_id automatically assigned to every record
A definition that groups one or more identifier entries used to identify CIs of a given class
A label printed on physical hardware assets
The reconciliation precedence number for a data source

rationale: A CI Identifier is the class-level definition that holds the identifier entries (the ordered sets of criterion attributes) IRE evaluates to match incoming data to existing CIs. Independent vs dependent identifiers determine whether a CI can be identified on its own or only in the context of a related CI.

distractor_notes.A: sys_id is the platform's internal record key; the CI Identifier is a configurable matching definition, not the sys_id.
distractor_notes.C: Asset tags are physical labels, unrelated to the IRE identifier construct.
distractor_notes.D: Source precedence is part of reconciliation, not the identifier definition itself.

stem: A database instance CI cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone — it only makes sense in the context of the server that hosts it. Which IRE concept models this?

options.text: An independent identifier
A dependent identifier (identification using a related parent CI)
A reconciliation exclusion
A data certification task

rationale: Dependent identifiers handle CIs that aren't unique on their own. The engine identifies them only in combination with a qualifying related CI (e.g., the hosting server), using the relationship plus the dependent CI's attributes to pin down identity.

distractor_notes.A: An independent identifier would assume the CI is uniquely identifiable by its own attributes — exactly what's not true here.
distractor_notes.C: Reconciliation governs which source writes attributes, not contextual identity.
distractor_notes.D: Certification is a human verification process, not an identity-resolution mechanism.

stem: What is the purpose of a CMDB data manager / CMDB policy applied through governance tooling?

options.text: To define repeatable, condition-based rules that enforce how CI data is maintained, retired, or cleaned up
To replace the need for any Discovery source
To grant every user admin rights to the CMDB
To disable relationships between CIs

rationale: Policies turn governance intent into automated, repeatable enforcement: conditions select the CIs, actions define what happens (retire, archive, remediate), and the rule runs consistently so quality standards aren't dependent on someone remembering to act.

distractor_notes.B: Policies govern data already in the CMDB; they don't substitute for ingestion sources.
distractor_notes.C: Governance restricts and assigns responsibility — it doesn't hand admin to everyone.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling relationships would damage the service model; that's not what policies are for.

stem: Which TWO outcomes can IRE produce when it processes an incoming CI payload?

options.text: Update an existing CI it matched via identifier entries
Insert a new CI when no match is found
Automatically write a new Discovery pattern
Generate a CMDB Health dashboard tab

rationale: IRE's core job at ingestion is identity resolution: match-and-update an existing CI, or insert a new one when nothing matches (and flag duplicates/errors when the data is ambiguous). Authoring patterns and building dashboards are unrelated functions.

distractor_notes.C: Pattern authoring is a Discovery design task; IRE never writes patterns.
distractor_notes.D: Dashboard tabs are part of CMDB Health configuration, not IRE processing output.

stem: A certification schedule completes and a user marks several CIs as failing certification. What is the intended next step in the governance loop?

options.text: The failed CIs are automatically deleted
The discrepancies are remediated/corrected so the data once again reflects reality
IRE re-runs all identification rules platform-wide
The CMDB Health score is permanently locked

rationale: Certification is a detect step; remediation is the act. A failed certification flags data that no longer matches reality, and the governance loop closes when someone corrects the record (or the underlying source). Failing certification doesn't delete CIs or trigger platform-wide rule reruns.

distractor_notes.A: Failing certification signals 'fix me', not 'destroy me' — deletion is a deliberate lifecycle action.
distractor_notes.C: Certification results don't cascade into a global IRE rerun.
distractor_notes.D: Health scores recompute on each scan; certification doesn't lock them.

stem: Which role is typically responsible for the day-to-day operational health of the CMDB — monitoring quality, triaging remediation, and running lifecycle actions?

options.text: The Configuration / CMDB Manager
The end user who opens incidents
The network firewall
The change approver board only

rationale: Above the strategic governance board sits an operational owner — the Configuration/CMDB Manager — who lives in the health dashboards and workspace, drives remediation, oversees certification, and executes lifecycle policy. They turn governance standards into daily upkeep.

distractor_notes.B: Incident users consume services; they don't own CMDB operational health.
distractor_notes.C: A firewall is infrastructure, not a governance role.
distractor_notes.D: The CAB approves changes; it isn't the steward of CMDB data quality.

stem: Why is it strongly recommended that all data entering the CMDB — Discovery, integrations, imports — go through IRE rather than writing directly to CI tables?

options.text: Because IRE is faster than a direct insert in every case
Because IRE enforces consistent identification and reconciliation
Because direct inserts are technically impossible
Because IRE encrypts the CI data

rationale: IRE is the single front door to the CMDB. Routing every source through it means the same identification logic prevents duplicate CIs and the same reconciliation rules stop a weak source from overwriting authoritative data. Bypassing it is the fastest way to corrupt the CMDB.

distractor_notes.A: The benefit is data integrity and consistency, not raw speed — IRE adds processing.
distractor_notes.C: Direct inserts are possible; they're just strongly discouraged because they skip governance.
distractor_notes.D: IRE governs identity and reconciliation; it isn't an encryption layer.

references.title: IRE as the single entry point

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Which sequence correctly reflects the escalating CI lifecycle actions managed by CMDB Data Manager?

options.text: Destroy → Archive → Retire
Retire → Archive → Destroy
Archive → Retire → Discover
Certify → Reconcile → Identify

rationale: The lifecycle escalates in finality: first Retire (mark the CI out of active operation), then Archive (move it off active tables but keep it recoverable), then Destroy (permanent removal). Each stage is a more irreversible step than the last.

distractor_notes.A: Reversed — you don't destroy before retiring; that's the opposite of controlled retirement.
distractor_notes.C: Discover is an ingestion action, not the tail end of a retirement lifecycle.
distractor_notes.D: Those are IRE/certification concepts, not the retire/archive/destroy lifecycle.

stem: Your governance standard says no CI may be created without an owner and a support group populated. Which approach best enforces this at the point of data entry?

options.text: A mandatory-attribute data policy / required fields enforced for the CI class
A weekly email reminding people to fill in owners
Deleting any CI that lacks an owner once a month
Turning off Discovery so no CIs are created

rationale: Enforcement at entry beats clean-up after the fact. Defining the attributes as mandatory (via data policy / required-field governance on the class) prevents incomplete CIs from being saved in the first place, which is exactly the governance principle of preventing bad data rather than chasing it.

distractor_notes.B: Reminders rely on human diligence and let bad data in — weak governance.
distractor_notes.C: Mass-deleting incomplete CIs destroys potentially real infrastructure records; prevention is preferred.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling Discovery sacrifices the CMDB's whole purpose to avoid a data-quality rule.

stem: In IRE, what is a 'data source' (discovery source) and why does it matter for reconciliation?

options.text: It is the name identifying which integration/process supplied the data, used to enforce attribute authority
It is the physical disk where the CMDB is stored
It is the user who last viewed the CI
It is the CI's install status

rationale: Each payload carries a data source (e.g., 'ServiceNow', a specific Service Graph Connector, an import). Reconciliation rules reference these sources to decide who's authoritative for which attributes — so identifying the source is what makes 'don't let source X overwrite source Y' possible.

distractor_notes.B: Data source is a logical origin label, not physical storage.
distractor_notes.C: Viewing a CI doesn't make someone a data source.
distractor_notes.D: Install status is an attribute value, not the origin of the data.

stem: A CMDB manager sees a spike in 'orphan' CIs (CIs with no relationships). From a governance standpoint, why are orphan CIs a remediation concern?

options.text: They consume too much disk space
Without relationships they can't participate in service maps or impact analysis
They automatically delete related incidents
They prevent users from logging in

rationale: The CMDB earns its keep through relationships — they power service mapping, impact analysis, and dependency views. An orphan CI is data with no context: it can't show what it supports or depends on, so relationship health is a core governance KPI and orphans are flagged for remediation.

distractor_notes.A: Storage is trivial; the real cost is lost analytical value, not disk.
distractor_notes.C: Orphan CIs don't delete incidents.
distractor_notes.D: CIs have nothing to do with user authentication.

stem: Data Certification is best categorized as which type of data-quality control?

options.text: An automated machine-discovery control
A manual / human attestation control complementing automated scanning
A network security control
A backup and recovery control

rationale: Automated scans catch what machines can see; certification covers what they can't — business ownership, accuracy of human-maintained fields, contextual correctness. It's a manual attestation layer that complements Discovery and Health, closing gaps automation alone leaves.

distractor_notes.A: Certification is explicitly the human counterpart to automated discovery, not another machine scan.
distractor_notes.C: It governs data accuracy, not network security.
distractor_notes.D: It has nothing to do with backups.

stem: An import keeps creating duplicate CIs because its payload lacks the attribute used in the class's identifier entry. What is the correct governance fix?

options.text: Disable IRE for that import so it inserts everything
Ensure the payload provides the criterion attributes the identifier needs
Delete the class so the import can't run
Lower the CMDB Health threshold so duplicates don't show

rationale: Duplicates from a payload usually mean IRE has nothing reliable to match on. The fix is to supply the criterion attributes the identifier expects (or revise the identification rule to match what the source can provide) so IRE can resolve identity instead of inserting new records.

distractor_notes.A: Disabling IRE removes the guardrail and guarantees more duplicates — the opposite of governance.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting the class destroys legitimate CIs and doesn't address the matching gap.
distractor_notes.D: Hiding duplicates on a dashboard doesn't fix the underlying identity problem.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: CMDB Data Manager improves on legacy ad-hoc cleanup scripts primarily because it provides what?

options.text: A governed, policy-driven, auditable framework for managing CI lifecycle at scale
Faster network discovery
A replacement for the change management process
Automatic creation of business services

rationale: The value of Data Manager is governance, not magic: lifecycle actions become declarative policies with conditions, previews, scheduling, and an audit trail — repeatable and consistent — instead of one-off scripts that are hard to review, easy to get wrong, and invisible after they run.

distractor_notes.B: Data Manager manages existing CIs' lifecycle; it doesn't perform network discovery.
distractor_notes.C: It complements but does not replace change management.
distractor_notes.D: Building business services is a CSDM/service-modeling activity, not a Data Manager function.

stem: What problem does Multisource CMDB solve for governance teams?

options.text: It hides all but one data source from the CI form
It records, per attribute, the value reported by each contributing source alongside the reconciled value
It prevents Discovery from ever updating a CI
It deletes any CI touched by more than one source

rationale: Multisource CMDB keeps a per-source record of what each integration reported for an attribute and what the reconciled (winning) value is. That transparency lets governance teams see exactly where sources disagree and why a particular value won, instead of silently overwriting and losing the trail.

distractor_notes.A: It surfaces source contributions rather than hiding them — the opposite of obscuring sources.
distractor_notes.C: It doesn't block Discovery; it records what Discovery and other sources each reported.
distractor_notes.D: Multiple sources on one CI is normal and expected; nothing is deleted for it.

stem: What is the purpose of a CMDB datasource precedence (reconciliation precedence) configuration?

options.text: To rank sources so the most authoritative one wins when several report the same attribute
To order CI classes alphabetically
To decide which dashboard loads first
To set the polling interval of the MID Server

rationale: When several sources can write the same attribute, precedence breaks the tie: the higher-precedence (more authoritative) source's value is retained. It's the practical lever governance uses to make reconciliation deterministic rather than last-write-wins.

distractor_notes.B: Class ordering is unrelated to source precedence.
distractor_notes.C: Dashboard load order has nothing to do with reconciliation precedence.
distractor_notes.D: MID Server polling is a Discovery/integration setting, not reconciliation precedence.

stem: You want to scope a set of CIs (e.g., all CIs supporting a specific application) so governance actions and reporting can target exactly that population. Which feature lets you define and reuse such a scoped set?

options.text: CMDB Groups
A Discovery schedule
A business rule on the incident table
A UI policy

rationale: CMDB Groups define a reusable, query-based set of CIs. Once defined, that group can drive remediation, certification, reporting, and Data Manager actions against precisely the population you care about, instead of rebuilding the same filter every time.

distractor_notes.B: A Discovery schedule controls when scanning runs, not a reusable governance population.
distractor_notes.C: Incident business rules act on incidents, not CMDB scoping.
distractor_notes.D: UI policies control form behavior, not CI population scoping.

stem: CMDB remediation typically begins from which trigger?

options.text: A CMDB Health KPI or rule flagging CIs that violate a quality standard
A user changing their password
A successful login to the instance
Closing an unrelated incident

rationale: Remediation is the action arm of Insight. Health metrics and rules detect CIs that fail completeness, compliance, or correctness standards, and those findings feed remediation queues where owners fix the data. Detection drives remediation; that's the governance loop.

distractor_notes.B: Password changes are identity events, unrelated to CMDB data quality.
distractor_notes.C: A login doesn't indicate a data-quality issue to remediate.
distractor_notes.D: Closing an unrelated incident doesn't surface a CMDB defect.

stem: A reconciliation rule names 'SCCM Integration' as authoritative for the OS attribute on servers. Discovery later reports a different OS value. What happens?

options.text: Discovery's OS value overwrites the SCCM value because Discovery always wins
The SCCM-sourced OS value is retained
The CI is deleted due to the conflict
Both values are concatenated into one string

rationale: That's the entire point of reconciliation: the rule designates SCCM as authoritative for OS, so Discovery — though it can update other attributes — cannot clobber the OS field. The authoritative source's value stands, keeping the attribute trustworthy.

distractor_notes.A: Discovery does not automatically win; reconciliation rules override that assumption per attribute.
distractor_notes.C: Conflicting attribute values don't delete CIs.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation keeps a single authoritative value; it doesn't concatenate.

stem: Which TWO are core responsibilities of CMDB governance (as opposed to one-off implementation tasks)?

options.text: Defining and maintaining data quality standards and ownership
Continuously monitoring CMDB health and driving remediation
Writing the application's source code
Designing the company's office network cabling

rationale: Governance is about standards and continuous upkeep: define what 'good data' means and who owns it, then keep watching health and remediating drift. Coding applications and cabling offices are unrelated engineering activities, not CMDB governance.

distractor_notes.C: Application development is unrelated to maintaining CMDB data quality.
distractor_notes.D: Physical cabling is infrastructure work, not data governance.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: A compliance requirement says retired servers must be kept for audit for two years before permanent deletion. How should this be modeled in CMDB Data Manager?

options.text: Destroy the CIs immediately on retirement
Retire on decommission, archive for the retention window, then destroy after two years
Never retire them, just hide them from reports
Delete them but keep a screenshot

rationale: The lifecycle maps neatly to the requirement: retire when decommissioned, archive to retain a recoverable, audit-friendly copy through the two-year window, then destroy once the retention period lapses. Data Manager schedules each transition on conditions so it happens automatically and consistently.

distractor_notes.A: Immediate destruction violates the two-year audit retention requirement.
distractor_notes.C: Hiding from reports doesn't satisfy retention or proper lifecycle governance.
distractor_notes.D: A screenshot is not an auditable, recoverable record of the CI.

stem: What is an IRE 'inclusion rule' (independent CI inclusion) used for?

options.text: To control which CIs/payload items IRE will process or skip based on defined conditions
To include extra columns on a list view
To add a CI to a change request
To include a user in an assignment group

rationale: Inclusion (and exclusion) rules let governance decide what IRE acts on — filtering or qualifying the payload items the engine should process versus ignore. They give fine-grained control so unwanted or low-quality records don't flow into the CMDB.

distractor_notes.B: List view columns are a UI concern, not IRE processing.
distractor_notes.C: Adding CIs to changes is a change-management activity.
distractor_notes.D: Group membership is access/assignment, unrelated to IRE.

stem: Which best describes the governance value of standardizing CI names and attributes through naming/data conventions?

options.text: It makes the CMDB look colorful
Consistent naming improves identification accuracy, reduces duplicates
It lets you skip IRE entirely
It increases the number of CIs

rationale: Conventions aren't cosmetic. Consistent names and attribute formats help IRE match records correctly (fewer duplicates), make data readable and joinable across ITSM/ITOM, and reduce the manual cleanup burden — all core governance wins.

distractor_notes.A: Appearance is irrelevant; the benefit is data integrity and usability.
distractor_notes.C: Standards complement IRE; they don't replace identity resolution.
distractor_notes.D: Good conventions tend to reduce duplicate inflation, not increase CI counts.

stem: When configuring Data Certification, what does the 'filter' on a certification template primarily determine?

options.text: Which CIs/records are selected for the certification tasks
The color of the certification banner
How fast the MID Server runs
The CMDB Health refresh rate

rationale: The filter defines the population — which records the certification campaign will ask owners to verify. Scope it well and the right people review the right CIs; scope it poorly and you either miss data or overwhelm reviewers.

distractor_notes.B: There's no governance value in banner color; the filter is about record selection.
distractor_notes.C: MID Server performance is unrelated to certification filters.
distractor_notes.D: Health refresh cadence is a separate setting.

stem: Why does ServiceNow recommend driving remediation from a prioritized, role-based workspace rather than from raw table edits?

options.text: Because raw tables are read-only
Because a workspace surfaces the highest-impact issues, tracks ownership
Because table edits are illegal
Because the workspace prevents Discovery from running

rationale: A workspace turns remediation into managed work: it ranks issues by impact, assigns and tracks owners, offers guided fixes, and leaves an audit trail. Ad-hoc table edits do the change but skip prioritization, accountability, and traceability — the governance parts.

distractor_notes.A: CMDB tables are editable; the issue is governance, not technical lock.
distractor_notes.C: Editing tables isn't illegal — it's just ungoverned.
distractor_notes.D: The workspace doesn't stop Discovery; it organizes remediation.

stem: During ingestion IRE finds a payload whose criterion attributes match more than one existing CI. How is this best characterized?

options.text: A clean single match that updates one CI
An ambiguous/multiple-match condition that should be surfaced for review rather than blindly updated
A signal to delete all matching CIs
A normal event requiring no governance attention

rationale: Matching multiple CIs means identity is ambiguous — often a symptom of pre-existing duplicates or weak identifiers. IRE flags these rather than guessing, so governance can resolve the ambiguity (merge duplicates, tighten identifiers) instead of silently corrupting a record.

distractor_notes.A: It's specifically not a clean single match — several CIs qualified.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting all matches would destroy legitimate data; review and merge is correct.
distractor_notes.D: Ambiguous matches absolutely warrant attention; ignoring them entrenches duplicates.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Which install_status value typically reflects a CI that is no longer in active operational use but is being kept for the moment?

options.text: Installed / In Use
Retired
On Order
Pending Install

rationale: Retired marks a CI that has been taken out of active service. It's the lifecycle state that precedes archival or destruction and keeps the record visible (but clearly inactive) so reporting and impact analysis don't treat it as live.

distractor_notes.A: Installed/In Use indicates an active CI, the opposite of retired.
distractor_notes.C: On Order is a procurement state before the CI exists operationally.
distractor_notes.D: Pending Install precedes go-live, not retirement.

stem: Leadership asks for one metric to summarize whether the CMDB can be trusted for decision-making. Which governance concept best answers that?

options.text: Number of CIs in the database
Overall CMDB Health score
Number of users with admin rights
Total disk used by cmdb tables

rationale: Trustworthiness is quality, not quantity. The CMDB Health score rolls completeness, compliance, and correctness into a defensible measure of how reliable the data is — exactly the kind of summary governance reports upward. Raw CI counts say nothing about accuracy.

distractor_notes.A: A big CMDB full of bad data is worse than a small accurate one; counts don't equal trust.
distractor_notes.C: Admin headcount is a security metric, not a data-trust metric.
distractor_notes.D: Storage size is irrelevant to whether the data is correct.

stem: IRE is exposed to integrations primarily through which mechanism so external sources can submit CI data for identification and reconciliation?

options.text: The Identification and Reconciliation API
The email inbound action processor
The knowledge base search API
The survey engine

rationale: External sources submit payloads to IRE through its API (the CMDB Instance / Identification and Reconciliation web service, e.g., createOrUpdateCI). This is what lets Service Graph Connectors and custom integrations get the benefit of identification and reconciliation rather than writing straight to tables.

distractor_notes.B: Inbound email actions process emails, not CI identification payloads.
distractor_notes.C: Knowledge search is unrelated to CMDB ingestion.
distractor_notes.D: The survey engine has nothing to do with IRE.

stem: Governance wants to prevent low-trust integrations from creating brand-new CI classes they shouldn't own, while still letting them update existing CIs. Which IRE capability supports this?

options.text: Reconciliation precedence only
Data source rules / IRE rules that restrict whether a source may insert
CMDB Health remediation tasks
Data Certification schedules

rationale: IRE data source rules can constrain what a given source is permitted to do — for instance allowing updates but blocking new CI creation for classes it shouldn't own. That keeps weak sources from polluting the CMDB with records they have no authority to create.

distractor_notes.A: Precedence arbitrates attribute values; it doesn't by itself gate insert-vs-update permission.
distractor_notes.C: Remediation cleans up after the fact; the goal here is prevention at ingestion.
distractor_notes.D: Certification verifies existing data; it doesn't control source insert rights.

stem: A 'suggested remediation' surfaced by CMDB tooling is best acted on how, from a governance perspective?

options.text: Auto-applied without review in every case
Reviewed by an owner, then applied or rejected with the decision tracked
Ignored, since suggestions are never useful
Escalated directly to the CEO

rationale: Suggestions accelerate remediation but governance keeps a human in the loop: an owner reviews the proposed fix, applies or rejects it, and the decision is recorded. That balances speed with accountability and prevents automated suggestions from silently changing trusted data.

distractor_notes.A: Blind auto-apply removes accountability and risks bad bulk changes.
distractor_notes.C: Suggestions are valuable inputs; ignoring them wastes the tooling.
distractor_notes.D: Routine data fixes don't belong on the CEO's desk.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: After a data center decommission, hundreds of CIs need to move through retirement consistently. Why is doing this via a Data Manager policy preferable to having each team retire their own CIs manually?

options.text: Manual retirement is impossible in ServiceNow
A policy applies the same rules, conditions, and downstream actions uniformly and leaves an audit trail
Policies retire CIs faster than the speed of light
Manual retirement deletes the entire CMDB

rationale: Scale plus consistency is the argument. A policy guarantees every CI in scope is handled the same way, with the same conditions and follow-on archive/destroy timing, all logged. Hundreds of teams retiring CIs by hand produces uneven states, missed relationships, and no central record.

distractor_notes.A: Manual retirement is possible — it's just inconsistent at scale.
distractor_notes.C: Speed framing is nonsense; the benefit is consistency and auditability.
distractor_notes.D: Manual retirement doesn't wipe the CMDB.

stem: What is the relationship between IRE and CI Class Manager identification rules?

options.text: They are unrelated subsystems
CI Class Manager is where identification and reconciliation rules for classes are viewed and maintained
CI Class Manager replaces IRE entirely
IRE rules can only be edited by exporting XML

rationale: CI Class Manager is the admin surface — it presents each class's identification rules, reconciliation rules, identifier entries, and dependent relationships in one place. IRE is the runtime that applies those definitions during ingestion. Design in Class Manager, execution in IRE.

distractor_notes.A: They're tightly coupled: one configures, the other executes.
distractor_notes.C: Class Manager configures rules; it doesn't replace the engine that runs them.
distractor_notes.D: Rules are maintained through the Class Manager UI, not only via XML export.

stem: Which statement reflects the recommended governance stance on manual CI creation by end users?

options.text: Anyone should be able to create any CI freely with no controls
Manual creation should be controlled and validated
Manual CI creation should never be allowed under any circumstance
Manual CIs don't need to pass through IRE

rationale: Manual entry has a place (for things automation can't see) but it's a common source of duplicates and gaps. Governance keeps it controlled: restrict who can create, require key attributes, and still route through IRE — so manual records meet the same standards as automated ones.

distractor_notes.A: Uncontrolled manual creation is a top cause of poor CMDB quality.
distractor_notes.C: An outright ban is impractical; some CIs must be entered manually.
distractor_notes.D: Manual creation should also benefit from IRE identification to avoid duplicates.

stem: A governance analyst sees that an attribute's reconciled value differs from what one trusted source reported. Where does Multisource CMDB help them investigate?

options.text: It shows the per-source reported values and which source won, so the analyst can see why the reconciled value is what it is
It rolls back the CMDB to yesterday
It emails every source owner automatically
It deletes the conflicting attribute

rationale: Multisource keeps the contribution history visible: each source's reported value plus the reconciled outcome. The analyst can see precisely which source was authoritative and what each claimed, turning a mysterious value into an explainable reconciliation decision.

distractor_notes.B: It's a transparency feature, not a time-machine rollback.
distractor_notes.C: It doesn't auto-notify source owners.
distractor_notes.D: It preserves and explains values; it doesn't delete the attribute.

stem: How does Data Certification differ from CMDB Health in terms of how a record is judged correct?

options.text: Certification relies on a human attesting to accuracy
They are exactly the same feature with two names
Health requires manual sign-off and certification is automated
Neither involves any rules or people

rationale: The distinction is human vs machine judgment. Certification asks a responsible person to vouch for the data; Health computes scores automatically against completeness/compliance/correctness rules. Used together they cover both what automation can measure and what only a human can confirm.

distractor_notes.B: They are complementary, distinct controls, not the same feature.
distractor_notes.C: Reversed — Health is automated, certification is the manual attestation.
distractor_notes.D: Both involve rules/criteria; certification also involves people.

stem: An organization wants every Service Graph Connector and custom integration to avoid creating duplicates and to respect attribute authority. What is the single most important architectural rule to enforce?

options.text: Let each integration write directly to cmdb_ci for speed
Require all sources to submit through IRE so identification and reconciliation always apply
Give each integration its own duplicate CMDB
Disable identification rules to avoid match errors

rationale: One rule prevents most CMDB chaos: everything goes through IRE. Centralizing ingestion means identification stops duplicates and reconciliation protects authoritative attributes uniformly, no matter how many connectors feed the CMDB. Bypassing IRE for any source breaks that guarantee.

distractor_notes.A: Direct writes skip the very protections you want and breed duplicates.
distractor_notes.C: Separate CMDBs fragment the single source of truth — the opposite goal.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling identification removes duplicate prevention entirely.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Which is a key benefit of archiving (rather than immediately destroying) CIs that have been retired?

options.text: It permanently and irreversibly removes the data
It removes CIs from active operational use while preserving a recoverable record for audit or historical analysis
It republishes the CIs as active
It converts the CIs into incidents

rationale: Archiving is the middle ground: the CI leaves active tables so it stops cluttering operational views and reports, yet a recoverable copy remains for audit, compliance, or trend analysis. You get cleanliness now without losing history — and can still destroy later if policy requires.

distractor_notes.A: That describes destroy, not archive — archive is recoverable.
distractor_notes.C: Archiving deactivates; it doesn't republish CIs as active.
distractor_notes.D: CIs aren't transformed into incidents by archiving.

stem: Which best describes the 'single source of truth' principle that CMDB governance protects?

options.text: Every team keeps its own independent copy of infrastructure data
One reconciled, trusted CMDB that all processes reference, rather than competing data silos
Only Discovery may ever read the CMDB
The CMDB is locked and never updated

rationale: Governance defends a single, reconciled CMDB that ITSM, ITOM, security, and reporting all rely on. The value collapses the moment teams maintain rival spreadsheets and shadow databases — decisions then rest on conflicting data. One trusted, continuously reconciled source is the goal.

distractor_notes.A: Independent copies are exactly the silos governance exists to eliminate.
distractor_notes.C: Many processes read the CMDB; Discovery is just one writer.
distractor_notes.D: A trusted CMDB is continuously updated, not frozen.

references.title: CMDB as single source of truth

stem: A class has two identifier entries: one on serial_number (priority 1) and one on name (priority 2). An incoming payload has a matching serial_number but a different name. What does IRE do?

options.text: Treats it as a match on the higher-priority serial_number entry and updates that CI
Creates a new CI because the name differs
Rejects the payload outright
Ignores serial_number and matches on name only

rationale: IRE evaluates identifier entries in priority order. A hit on the higher-priority serial_number entry resolves identity, so it updates that existing CI — and a changed name is just an attribute update, not a reason to spawn a duplicate. Ordering identifiers by reliability is exactly how you avoid duplicates.

distractor_notes.B: A differing lower-priority attribute doesn't override a strong higher-priority match.
distractor_notes.C: A valid match isn't rejected; it's updated.
distractor_notes.D: The priority order means serial_number is tried first, not ignored.

stem: Which TWO are typical categories of issues a CMDB manager remediates from health findings?

options.text: CIs missing required attributes
Duplicate CIs that should be merged
Slow internet at a branch office
An employee's expense report

rationale: Remediation targets data defects: completeness gaps (missing required attributes) and duplicate records are two of the most common. Branch internet speed and expense reports are operational/finance matters with nothing to do with CMDB data quality.

distractor_notes.C: Network performance is an infrastructure issue, not a CMDB data defect.
distractor_notes.D: Expense reports are a finance process, unrelated to CI quality.

stem: Governance decides that only the HR integration may set the 'managed by' field on employee-owned laptops. What is the cleanest way to enforce this across all sources?

options.text: A reconciliation rule designating the HR source as authoritative for that attribute
An email policy reminding people not to edit the field
Deleting the field from the table
A UI macro on the laptop form

rationale: Attribute-level authority is exactly what reconciliation rules express. Naming the HR integration authoritative for 'managed by' means every other source is blocked from overwriting it at the engine level — enforcement that holds regardless of which integration tries to write.

distractor_notes.B: Reminders don't enforce anything technically and won't stop integrations.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting the field destroys needed data instead of governing who writes it.
distractor_notes.D: A form macro only affects manual UI use, not API/integration writes.

stem: On what basis are Data Certification tasks typically generated on a recurring cadence?

options.text: Randomly, with no schedule
On a defined schedule/frequency so data is re-verified periodically before it goes stale
Only when an incident is opened
Only during system upgrades

rationale: Certification is scheduled so verification keeps pace with drift — monthly, quarterly, or whatever cadence fits the data's volatility. Periodic re-attestation is what stops human-maintained fields from quietly becoming wrong between automated scans.

distractor_notes.A: Randomness defeats the purpose; certification is deliberately scheduled.
distractor_notes.C: Certification isn't incident-triggered; it's a proactive cadence.
distractor_notes.D: Tying it only to upgrades would leave long verification gaps.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: A Data Manager policy is set to destroy CIs 30 days after archival, but auditors now require 1 year retention. What is the correct governance response?

options.text: Update the policy's retention condition to 1 year so the change applies consistently going forward
Manually un-delete CIs each month
Disable Data Manager entirely
Switch all CIs back to active

rationale: Because the lifecycle lives in policy, compliance changes are a policy edit: extend the destroy condition to one year and every in-scope CI now follows the new rule automatically. That's the payoff of declarative lifecycle management over scattered manual deletions.

distractor_notes.B: Manual un-deletion is error-prone and doesn't fix the policy that caused early destruction.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling Data Manager abandons governance instead of adjusting it.
distractor_notes.D: Reactivating retired CIs misrepresents their real state.

stem: What is the consequence of having no (or weak) identification rules on a CI class?

options.text: Faster, cleaner data with fewer records
IRE cannot reliably match incoming data
The class becomes read-only
CMDB Health automatically reaches 100%

rationale: Identification rules are how IRE recognizes 'this is the same CI.' Without a strong rule, the engine has nothing dependable to match on and keeps inserting new records for things that already exist — the classic root cause of duplicate sprawl.

distractor_notes.A: Weak identification produces more (duplicate) records, not fewer/cleaner ones.
distractor_notes.C: Missing rules don't lock the class; they degrade matching.
distractor_notes.D: Duplicates would lower health, not push it to a perfect score.

stem: Which document or agreement typically captures the agreed scope, ownership, and quality targets for the CMDB?

options.text: A CMDB governance policy / data management charter
The firewall ruleset
A user's mailbox rules
The incident SLA definition

rationale: A governance policy or charter is where scope, ownership, roles, and measurable quality targets are written down and agreed. It's the reference point that makes accountability real — without it, 'who owns this data and how good must it be' stays a matter of opinion.

distractor_notes.B: Firewall rules govern network traffic, not CMDB data ownership.
distractor_notes.C: Mailbox rules are personal email settings.
distractor_notes.D: Incident SLAs govern incident response times, not CMDB quality targets.

stem: A health rule flags 5,000 CIs missing an owner. Remediating all at once is impractical. What governance approach keeps progress measurable?

options.text: Ignore the finding because it's too large
Prioritize by impact (e.g., CIs supporting critical services first), assign owners, and track remediation over time
Delete all 5,000 CIs
Set the health threshold to zero so nothing is flagged

rationale: Big findings get triaged, not abandoned. Rank by business impact so the CIs underpinning critical services are fixed first, assign clear owners, and watch the metric improve. That converts an overwhelming number into a managed, trackable program of work.

distractor_notes.A: Ignoring it lets the quality gap persist and grow.
distractor_notes.C: Mass deletion destroys real infrastructure records to dodge a data-entry gap.
distractor_notes.D: Lowering thresholds hides the problem instead of fixing it.

stem: What does it mean that IRE is 'class-aware' when identifying CIs?

options.text: It uses the CI class (and its inheritance) to apply the correct identifier and reconciliation rules
It only works on the base cmdb_ci table and ignores classes
It identifies users, not CIs
It treats every CI as the same class

rationale: Rules are defined per class and inherited through the CMDB's class hierarchy, so IRE applies the right identifier and reconciliation logic for, say, a Linux server versus a database instance. Class-awareness is what lets identification be precise instead of one-size-fits-all.

distractor_notes.B: IRE works across the extended class model, not just the base table.
distractor_notes.C: IRE identifies configuration items, not user records.
distractor_notes.D: Treating all CIs identically would defeat class-specific identification.

stem: Business-owned attributes like 'business owner' and 'department' on critical application CIs are often wrong, yet Discovery can't see them. Which governance control is best suited to keep them accurate?

options.text: Data Certification campaigns routed to the responsible business owners
A faster Discovery schedule
A reconciliation rule naming Discovery authoritative
Deleting the attributes

rationale: When the truth lives in people's heads rather than on the network, certification is the right tool: it routes a verification task to the business owner who actually knows, on a recurring cadence. Automated scanning can't validate ownership or organizational context.

distractor_notes.B: Discovery can't see business ownership at all, so scanning faster won't help.
distractor_notes.C: Making Discovery authoritative for data it can't observe is meaningless.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting needed business attributes throws away information instead of maintaining it.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Before CMDB Data Manager, why was uncontrolled deletion of CIs considered risky?

options.text: It could remove relationships, break service maps, and erase audit history with no consistent process or trail
It made the CMDB load faster
It automatically improved data quality
It had no effect on anything

rationale: Ad-hoc deletion is dangerous because CIs are connected: dropping one can sever relationships that service maps and impact analysis depend on, and doing it without process leaves no audit trail and inconsistent results. Data Manager replaces that risk with governed, logged lifecycle actions.

distractor_notes.B: Marginal performance is irrelevant next to broken service maps and lost history.
distractor_notes.C: Reckless deletion degrades quality and trust; it doesn't improve it.
distractor_notes.D: Deletion has real, often damaging downstream effects.

stem: A team proposes letting a spreadsheet import overwrite serial numbers maintained by Discovery 'because the spreadsheet is newer.' From a governance view, what's the right principle to apply?

options.text: Newest write always wins, regardless of source
Authority should be based on which source is most reliable for that attribute, enforced by reconciliation
Spreadsheets are always authoritative
Serial numbers should never be stored

rationale: Recency is a poor proxy for accuracy. Governance assigns authority by trustworthiness for each attribute and lets reconciliation enforce it. If Discovery is the reliable source for serial numbers, a 'newer' but less trustworthy spreadsheet shouldn't be allowed to overwrite it.

distractor_notes.A: Last-write-wins is precisely the un-governed behavior reconciliation exists to prevent.
distractor_notes.C: Spreadsheets are typically less reliable than automated discovery for hardware facts.
distractor_notes.D: Serial numbers are valuable identifiers; the issue is who's authoritative, not whether to store them.

stem: Why is executive sponsorship considered important for a CMDB governance program?

options.text: Executives personally enter CI data
Sponsorship secures funding, cross-team cooperation, and authority to enforce standards that span organizational silos
It lets the program skip data quality entirely
It removes the need for any roles

rationale: CMDB governance crosses team boundaries, so it needs authority that crosses them too. Executive sponsorship provides the mandate, budget, and cooperation to enforce shared standards — without it, governance stalls whenever a team declines to participate.

distractor_notes.A: Executives sponsor and empower; they don't do the data entry.
distractor_notes.C: Sponsorship strengthens quality efforts; it doesn't waive them.
distractor_notes.D: Sponsorship complements defined roles rather than eliminating them.

stem: What is the governance advantage of tying remediation findings to owners/assignment groups rather than leaving them unassigned?

options.text: It guarantees the findings disappear on their own
Accountability — someone is responsible for fixing each issue, and progress can be tracked to closure
It hides the issues from reporting
It converts CIs into knowledge articles

rationale: Unowned work doesn't get done. Assigning each finding to an owner or group creates accountability and a closure path you can measure. It's the difference between a list of problems and a managed remediation program.

distractor_notes.A: Issues don't self-resolve; ownership is what drives fixes.
distractor_notes.C: Assignment makes work visible and trackable, not hidden.
distractor_notes.D: Remediation fixes CI data; it doesn't turn CIs into KB articles.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Which condition is the MOST appropriate trigger for a Data Manager retirement policy on infrastructure CIs?

options.text: The CI has not been updated/seen by any authoritative source for a defined stale period
The CI's name starts with the letter A
A random selection each day
Whenever any incident is closed

rationale: Staleness is the meaningful signal: if no authoritative source has confirmed a CI for a defined period, it's likely gone from the environment and is a sound retirement candidate. Arbitrary triggers like first-letter or randomness have no relationship to whether the CI still exists.

distractor_notes.B: A name's first letter says nothing about whether the asset still exists.
distractor_notes.C: Random retirement would remove live CIs and miss dead ones.
distractor_notes.D: Incident closure is unrelated to a CI's continued existence.

stem: What is 'CI reconciliation' best summarized as?

options.text: Deciding, when multiple sources report data for the same CI
Scanning the network for new devices
Designing the CMDB class hierarchy
Sending a survey to CI owners

rationale: Once identification says 'this is the same CI,' reconciliation arbitrates the data: among competing sources, which values win for which attributes. It's the governance mechanism that keeps a CI's record coherent when many systems contribute to it.

distractor_notes.B: Network scanning is Discovery; reconciliation acts on the data afterward.
distractor_notes.C: Class design is a Configuration-domain modeling task.
distractor_notes.D: Surveys relate to certification, not reconciliation.

stem: Governance wants to ensure retired CIs are excluded from CMDB Health completeness scoring so they don't distort metrics. What is the right way to handle this?

options.text: Scope health metrics/dashboards to active CIs
Delete every retired CI immediately
Turn off CMDB Health
Mark retired CIs as In Use

rationale: Metrics should measure the population you actually operate. Scoping health rules and dashboards to active CIs (excluding Retired) keeps the score honest without destroying records that are intentionally being retained for audit. It's a filtering decision, not a deletion one.

distractor_notes.B: Immediate deletion may violate retention and isn't necessary to fix scoring.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling Health removes the metric entirely instead of scoping it.
distractor_notes.D: Mislabeling retired CIs as In Use corrupts the data to fix a reporting view.

stem: A 'data owner' in CMDB governance is best defined as which of the following?

options.text: The person/role accountable for the accuracy and maintenance of a defined set of CI data
The vendor who sold the hardware
Any user who has ever viewed the CI
The MID Server service account

rationale: A data owner is accountable for a slice of CI data being correct and kept up to date — they're who certification routes to and who answers for quality in their domain. Ownership is about accountability, not who sold the gear or who happened to open the record.

distractor_notes.B: The hardware vendor has no accountability for your CMDB data accuracy.
distractor_notes.C: Viewing a record doesn't confer ownership responsibility.
distractor_notes.D: A service account executes integrations; it isn't an accountable data owner.

stem: After enabling a new integration, duplicate network gear CIs appear. Investigation shows the integration sends MAC addresses while the identifier expects serial numbers. The best governance fix is to?

options.text: Align identification — either have the integration supply serial numbers or add a reliable MAC-based identifier entry — so IRE can match correctly
Delete the network class
Stop all Discovery
Accept the duplicates as normal

rationale: Matching only works when the identifier and the payload speak the same language. Either get the integration to send the expected serial numbers, or extend the identifier with a trustworthy MAC-based entry. Then IRE resolves identity instead of minting duplicates.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting the class destroys legitimate CIs and ignores the matching gap.
distractor_notes.C: Stopping Discovery sacrifices core data to mask an identifier mismatch.
distractor_notes.D: Tolerating duplicates erodes the CMDB's trustworthiness.

stem: Which best captures the relationship between CMDB Health (Insight) and remediation (Govern)?

options.text: Health detects and measures data-quality problems
They are the same process under different names
Remediation detects problems and Health fixes them
Neither relates to data quality

rationale: Insight (Health) is the sensor; Govern (remediation) is the actuator. Health surfaces and quantifies completeness, compliance, and correctness issues; remediation assigns and resolves them. Detection without action is just reporting; the loop only closes when remediation follows.

distractor_notes.B: They're distinct, complementary stages — measurement vs action.
distractor_notes.C: Reversed — Health detects, remediation fixes.
distractor_notes.D: Both are squarely about CMDB data quality.

stem: Which outcome is a sign that a Data Certification program is working well over time?

options.text: Certification tasks are never completed
Recurring attestation keeps key attributes accurate and surfaces drift early
All CIs are deleted after each campaign
Discovery is no longer needed

rationale: A healthy certification program shows up as sustained accuracy: owners regularly confirm or correct data, drift gets caught before it spreads, and confidence in the CMDB rises. Completed tasks and steady or improving quality are the signals, not deletions or abandoning automated discovery.

distractor_notes.A: Uncompleted tasks signal a failing program, not a working one.
distractor_notes.C: Certification verifies data; it doesn't wipe CIs.
distractor_notes.D: Certification complements Discovery; it never replaces it.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Which TWO actions can a CMDB Data Manager policy be configured to perform on CIs that meet its conditions?

options.text: Retire the CIs
Archive or destroy the CIs
Reprogram the network switches
Generate marketing emails

rationale: Data Manager operates on the CI lifecycle: it can retire CIs and then archive or destroy them based on conditions. It does not configure physical network hardware or send marketing communications — those are outside the CMDB data lifecycle entirely.

distractor_notes.C: Configuring switches is network engineering, not CMDB lifecycle management.
distractor_notes.D: Marketing email is unrelated to CI lifecycle actions.

stem: Why does ServiceNow recommend reviewing and tuning out-of-box identification rules rather than assuming they fit every environment?

options.text: Because OOB rules are always wrong
Because each environment's data sources and attribute availability differ, so rules may need adjustment to match reliably and avoid duplicates
Because rules cannot be changed once shipped
Because tuning rules disables IRE

rationale: Out-of-box rules are a strong starting point, but the attributes your sources actually populate vary by environment. Reviewing and tuning the identifiers to your real data is how you keep matching accurate and prevent duplicates — a standard part of CMDB onboarding governance.

distractor_notes.A: OOB rules are sensible defaults, not always wrong — they just may need tuning.
distractor_notes.C: Identification rules are configurable, not frozen.
distractor_notes.D: Tuning rules refines IRE behavior; it doesn't disable the engine.

stem: Which governance practice most directly prevents 'CMDB sprawl' — uncontrolled growth of low-value or duplicate CIs?

options.text: Defining what should be in the CMDB
Allowing every tool to push everything it can see
Turning off all data sources
Never retiring anything

rationale: Sprawl is controlled at three points: decide what belongs in the CMDB (scope), force all ingestion through IRE so duplicates are caught, and run lifecycle management so dead CIs leave. Letting every tool dump everything and never retiring is exactly how sprawl happens.

distractor_notes.B: Ingesting everything indiscriminately is a primary cause of sprawl.
distractor_notes.C: Killing all sources leaves the CMDB empty and useless — an overcorrection.
distractor_notes.D: Never retiring lets dead CIs accumulate forever.

stem: An integration legitimately needs to correct a value that a reconciliation rule currently reserves for another source. What is the proper governance step?

options.text: Review and update the reconciliation rule
Bypass IRE and write the value directly to the table
Duplicate the CI so each source has its own copy
Delete the reconciliation rules entirely

rationale: Authority is a governance decision, so changing it is a governed change to the reconciliation rule — not a workaround. Update which source is authoritative for that attribute, and IRE will enforce the new, agreed authority consistently. Bypassing IRE or duplicating CIs just creates new problems.

distractor_notes.B: Direct writes defeat reconciliation and reintroduce uncontrolled overwrites.
distractor_notes.C: Duplicating CIs fragments the record and breaks the single source of truth.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting all reconciliation rules removes attribute protection everywhere.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: What is a 'definition' (policy definition) in CMDB Data Manager composed of, at a high level?

options.text: A target CI scope/condition plus the lifecycle action(s) and timing to apply
A list of users who can log in
A set of email templates
A network subnet range only

rationale: A Data Manager definition pairs a scope (which CIs, by condition) with actions (retire/archive/destroy) and timing. That structure is what makes lifecycle management declarative: say what to act on, what to do, and when, and the tool executes it consistently.

distractor_notes.B: Login access is a security/role concern, not a lifecycle definition.
distractor_notes.C: Email templates aren't the substance of a lifecycle policy.
distractor_notes.D: A subnet alone doesn't define CI scope plus lifecycle action and timing.

stem: A certification task asks an owner to verify 200 CIs, but they only have authority over 40 of them. What does this most likely indicate about the certification design?

options.text: The certification filter/scope or assignment is misaligned and should be refined to match actual ownership
Certification should be abandoned
The owner should certify all 200 regardless
The CMDB should be deleted

rationale: Certification only works when the right person reviews the right records. If an owner is handed CIs they don't control, the scope or assignment logic is off and should be refined so each reviewer gets the population they can actually vouch for. Forcing them to rubber-stamp the rest defeats the control.

distractor_notes.B: One misconfiguration is a tuning problem, not a reason to abandon certification.
distractor_notes.C: Certifying CIs you don't understand produces false assurance.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting the CMDB is wildly disproportionate to a scoping error.

stem: Why is an audit trail / history on CI changes important to CMDB governance?

options.text: It lets you trace who or what changed a value and when
It makes the CMDB load faster
It hides changes from auditors
It prevents any future changes

rationale: Trustworthy data needs traceability. An audit trail records who/what changed an attribute and when, which supports accountability, root-cause analysis when data looks wrong, and compliance evidence. Governance leans on this history to manage and defend data quality.

distractor_notes.B: Auditing is about traceability, not performance.
distractor_notes.C: An audit trail exposes changes to auditors — the opposite of hiding them.
distractor_notes.D: History records changes; it doesn't freeze the record.

stem: A governance review finds many de-duplication tasks piling up unworked. What is the risk of leaving them unresolved?

options.text: No risk; duplicates are harmless
Duplicate CIs distort reporting, impact analysis, and service maps
The instance will run out of memory immediately
All users will be locked out

rationale: Unmerged duplicates quietly corrupt everything that reads the CMDB: counts are inflated, impact analysis misses or double-counts dependencies, and service maps fracture. Working the de-duplication queue is how governance keeps the data — and the decisions made on it — trustworthy.

distractor_notes.A: Duplicates are far from harmless; they undermine the CMDB's core value.
distractor_notes.C: Duplicates degrade data quality, not instance memory in that dramatic way.
distractor_notes.D: Duplicate CIs don't affect user authentication.

stem: Which is the best example of a measurable CMDB governance KPI?

options.text: Percentage of CIs with a complete set of required attributes
The font used on the CI form
Number of coffee breaks the team takes
The color of the dashboard background

rationale: A useful governance KPI is quantifiable and tied to data quality — completeness (percent of CIs with required attributes filled) is a textbook example, alongside compliance and correctness rates. Cosmetic or irrelevant items can't tell you whether the CMDB is trustworthy.

distractor_notes.B: Form fonts have no bearing on data quality.
distractor_notes.C: Coffee breaks are unrelated to CMDB governance.
distractor_notes.D: Dashboard colors don't measure data trustworthiness.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: Which statement about relationships during CI retirement is correct from a governance standpoint?

options.text: Relationships should be handled deliberately, because retiring a CI affects the service maps and dependencies it participates in
Relationships are irrelevant when retiring CIs
Retiring a CI automatically improves all its relationships
Relationships must always be deleted before any CI can be viewed

rationale: Because CIs are nodes in a dependency graph, retiring one ripples into the service maps and impact paths it touches. Governed lifecycle management considers those relationships deliberately — exactly why controlled tooling beats blunt deletion that can silently break a service view.

distractor_notes.B: Relationships are highly relevant — they're what makes the CMDB valuable.
distractor_notes.C: Retirement doesn't magically improve relationships.
distractor_notes.D: Viewing a CI doesn't require deleting its relationships.

stem: Which TWO are true about IRE identifier entries?

options.text: An identifier entry contains one or more criterion attributes used to match CIs
Identifier entries can be ordered by priority so stronger matches are tried first
Identifier entries set the CMDB Health refresh schedule
Identifier entries define user login passwords

rationale: Identifier entries hold the criterion attributes IRE compares (e.g., serial number) and are evaluated in priority order so the most reliable match is attempted first. They have nothing to do with health scheduling or authentication.

distractor_notes.C: Health refresh cadence is a separate dashboard setting.
distractor_notes.D: Passwords are an identity/security concern, unrelated to CI identifier entries.

stem: To keep the de-duplication backlog from recurring, governance should focus most on which long-term action?

options.text: Strengthening identification rules and source data quality so duplicates aren't created in the first place
Merging duplicates faster and faster forever
Increasing the dashboard refresh rate
Hiding the de-duplication module

rationale: Merging duplicates treats the symptom; preventing them treats the cause. The durable fix is upstream — tighter identification rules and cleaner source payloads so IRE matches correctly and stops minting duplicates. Then the backlog shrinks naturally instead of being perpetually drained.

distractor_notes.B: Endless faster merging never addresses why duplicates keep appearing.
distractor_notes.C: Refresh rate doesn't change how many duplicates are created.
distractor_notes.D: Hiding the module conceals the problem rather than preventing it.

stem: How should CMDB governance treat the relationship between data quality and the CMDB's business value?

options.text: They are independent; value doesn't depend on quality
Business value depends directly on data quality
Only the size of the CMDB matters
Quality only matters for the IT team's internal use

rationale: Every consumer of the CMDB — change impact, incident routing, security posture, service mapping — is only as reliable as the data underneath. That's why governance frames data quality as the foundation of business value: improve the data and every dependent process gets more trustworthy.

distractor_notes.A: Value is tightly coupled to quality; bad data poisons every downstream use.
distractor_notes.C: Size without quality is a liability, not value.
distractor_notes.D: The CMDB's data underpins enterprise-wide processes, not just IT's own use.

subdomain: CMDB Data Manager and CI lifecycle
stem: A governance team wants assurance that lifecycle policies are actually running and acting on the intended CIs over time. What should they rely on?

options.text: Data Manager execution history/logs and policy run results, reviewed periodically
Assuming it works because it was set up once
Asking end users to guess
The color of the policy icon

rationale: Governance verifies rather than assumes. Data Manager records run history and results, so the team can periodically confirm policies executed, see how many CIs were acted on, and catch policies that silently stopped matching. 'Set it and forget it' is how governance quietly fails.

distractor_notes.B: Assuming continued success is exactly the blind spot reviews are meant to close.
distractor_notes.C: User guesses aren't evidence of policy execution.
distractor_notes.D: An icon color tells you nothing about whether policies ran.

stem: Two ingestion sources both report the same physical server, and you're worried about creating duplicate CIs. Which engine is responsible for matching them to a single CI?

options.text: The Identification and Reconciliation Engine
A transform map coalesce field only
A UI policy on the cmdb_ci form
The Service Portal

rationale: IRE applies identifier rules (like serial number or name+IP) to match incoming data to existing CIs, so multiple sources resolve to one record instead of duplicates. It's the gatekeeper for all CMDB writes, regardless of source.

distractor_notes.B: Coalesce helps a single import, but cross-source CI identity is IRE's job.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form behavior, not CI identification.
distractor_notes.D: The Service Portal is an end-user interface, unrelated to identification.

stem: A less-trusted integration keeps overwriting the operating-system attribute that Discovery populates accurately. How do you make Discovery the authority for that attribute?

options.text: Configure reconciliation rules so only Discovery can update that attribute
Delete the other data source
Add a watch list to the CI
Mark the attribute read-only on the form

rationale: Reconciliation rules define which data source is authoritative for specific attributes. Granting Discovery precedence for the OS attribute stops the weaker source from overwriting it, without removing that source entirely.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting the source is heavy-handed and loses its other useful data.
distractor_notes.C: Watch lists notify people; they don't govern attribute precedence.
distractor_notes.D: A read-only form field doesn't stop server-side ingestion from other sources.

stem: Governance wants CI owners to periodically confirm that key attributes on their CIs are still accurate. Which capability schedules and tracks these verification tasks?

options.text: Data Certification
A transform map
A coalesce field
The MID Server

rationale: Data Certification generates scheduled tasks asking responsible users to confirm (certify) that specified records/attributes are accurate, creating an auditable cadence for data quality. It's a governance staple for keeping the CMDB trustworthy.

distractor_notes.B: Transform maps move imported data; they don't run certification cycles.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches records on import.
distractor_notes.D: The MID Server bridges connectivity; it doesn't certify data.

stem: A data manager needs a single place to triage CMDB health issues and work de-duplication and remediation tasks. Where should they work?

options.text: CMDB Workspace
The Service Catalog
The Application Navigator favorites
An update set

rationale: CMDB Workspace centralizes health insights and remediation, including de-duplication tasks and Service Graph Connector status, so data managers can triage and act in one place.

distractor_notes.B: The Service Catalog is for requesting items, not CMDB remediation.
distractor_notes.C: Favorites are navigation shortcuts.
distractor_notes.D: Update sets move configuration between instances.

references.title: Service Graph Connector Central in CMDB Workspace

stem: IRE detects two CIs that appear to be the same asset. What does it generate so a data manager can resolve the duplication?

options.text: A de-duplication task
A change request
A knowledge article
A catalog item

rationale: When duplicates are detected, IRE/CMDB health creates de-duplication tasks that let a data manager review and merge the records to a single CI, cleaning up the duplication rather than guessing.

distractor_notes.B: A change request manages changes, not CI duplicate resolution.
distractor_notes.C: Knowledge articles document information.
distractor_notes.D: Catalog items are orderable services.

stem: Several sources report different values for the same CI attribute, and you want to see each source's value plus which one is authoritative. Which capability shows this?

options.text: Multisource CMDB (CMDB 360)
A coalesce field
A UI policy
The watch list
